title: How to Preach a Narrative Text
subtitle: How to preach a Bible story or narrative text faithfully, honoring plot, character, and tension instead of flattening the story into three points and a moral.

sections.title: We Were Taught to Flatten Stories
sections.body:
Most of the Bible is story, and most of us were trained to ruin it.

We learned to preach epistles. Find the proposition, divide it into points, support each point, apply. It is a fine method for Paul. Then we take that same machine to a narrative, to David and Goliath, to the woman at the well, to Jonah in the storm, and we grind a living story into three abstract principles and a moral. The plot becomes a delivery system for ideas, and the moment we have extracted the ideas, we throw the story away like packaging.

The trouble is that God did not give us a systematic theology of his dealings with the Ninevites. He gave us a reluctant prophet, a storm, a fish, a withered plant, and a question left hanging in the air. The form is the message. When you flatten the story into bullet points, you do not just lose the beauty. You lose the meaning, because the meaning was carried in the shape, and you threw the shape away.

sections.title: Preach the Story as a Story
sections.body:
A narrative makes its point through movement. Honor the movement.

Stories have shape. A setting, a tension that builds, a crisis, a turn, a resolution. The author is doing something with that shape. He withholds information to create suspense. He repeats a phrase to build a drumbeat. He puts two scenes side by side so the second comments on the first. He lets a character speak and lets the speech expose him. These are not decorations on top of the point. They are how the point is made.

So let your sermon follow the story rather than dismantle it. Often the best structure for preaching a narrative is the narrative itself, retold with skill, slowed down where the text slows down, accelerating where it races. You are not abandoning structure. You are borrowing the structure the author already built. The tension the story creates becomes the tension your sermon rides, and the resolution the story reaches becomes the place your sermon lands. Trust the form. The Holy Spirit chose it on purpose.

sections.title: Slow Down and Let Them See It
sections.body:
The power of a story is that it puts you inside it. Your job is to open the door and walk the people in.

We rush. We summarize the scene in a sentence so we can hurry to the lesson. And in the rushing we rob the people of the very thing a story does, which is to make them feel it before they understand it. Slow down. Let them stand on the hill and see the giant come down, nine feet of bronze and contempt, and feel the army shrink behind them. Let them sit at the well in the noon heat and feel why a woman would come to draw water at the hour no one else would, alone, hiding from the talk of the town.

This is not embellishment. The text gives you the details for a reason, and your task is to make the people see what is already there. Read closely enough to notice what the author noticed. The detail he lingers on, linger on. The silence he leaves, leave. Help them feel the fear, the shame, the hope, the dread, because a story understood without being felt has not been understood at all. The affections are where the narrative does its work.

sections.title: Find the Point Without Killing the Story
sections.body:
Honoring the story does not mean refusing to say what it means. It means finding the meaning the right way.

A narrative still has a point. The author is not merely entertaining. But you find that point by asking what the story is doing, not by stripping it for parts. Ask why this story, here, in this book. Ask what the narrator approves and what he quietly condemns, because biblical narrators rarely lecture, they show. Ask what the turn reveals about God, because the hero of every biblical story is finally God and not the human in the foreground.

This is the guardrail against moralizing. David and Goliath is not be brave and face your giants. That makes you David and reduces a story about God deliverer to a pep talk. The story is about a God who saves his helpless people through an unlikely deliverer he chose, and that points past David to a greater David who faced a greater enemy on a hill outside Jerusalem and won with no sword at all. Find the point along the grain of the whole story, and you preach the gospel the narrative was always carrying instead of a moral it never meant.

sections.title: A Working Method for Narrative
sections.body:
Preaching a story well is a craft you can practice. Here is a way in.

First, read it until you see it. Not for points. For pictures. Read the scene until you can stand inside it, until you notice the detail you skimmed the first ten times, until the characters are people and not symbols. The exegesis of a narrative begins with attention, not analysis.

Second, find the tension and the turn. Where does the story tighten. Where does it break open. Build your sermon around that movement rather than against it, so that your people feel the pressure rise and release the way the first hearers did.

Third, place it in the larger story. A single narrative is a scene in the one drama that runs from a garden to a city. Locate it there and the road to Christ usually opens on its own.

Finally, retell it so they live it, then land where it lands. Resist the urge to tidy what the author left open. If the story ends with a question, let your sermon end near that question. The story was inspired in its own shape. Preach it in that shape, and let it do to your people what it has always done.
